newsitem.title: UK: BT Q1 pre-tax profits seen falling.
newsitem.headline: BT Q1 pre-tax profits seen falling.

text.p: Rising competition, start-up costs of new operations and a charge for redundancies are expected to take their toll on first quarter profits from British Telecommunications Plc on Thursday.
Analysts have pencilled in pre-tax profits for BT of 830 to 860 million pounds -- including a redundancy charge of 20 to 75 million pounds -- compared to 869 million in the first quarter of 1996.
However, volume growth is generally expected to remain at around seven percent both for inland and international telephone calls.
Some analysts say that BT's profits will be mainly hit because its telephone line base is shrinking amid increasing competition from rivals such as cable companies, which is driving down prices.
Analysts say BT, which has about 27 million exchange lines of which 20.5 million are residential, is losing about 60,000 lines per month to the cable companies.
But in the past, the group has chased its cost base down quicker -- by reducing staff numbers -- than revenues have fallen.

"Whilst revenues are still falling, because tariffs are falling, they are not quite so easily being compensated for by laying off more people," noted one analyst, who declined to be named. "Because, frankly, there aren't that many people to lay off."

Some analysts say lower profits from BT are a manifestation that BT is no growth company as a stand-alone business. "All of the growth really comes from their international operations and when -- or if -- the merger with (America's) MCI goes through," noted the analyst.
BT faces many exceptional charges over the coming year -- including a 500 million stg windfall tax and additional pension costs to the wage line of around 150 million pounds.
The company must also take a 120 million pound charge for compensating option holders who do not receive a 35p special dividend in the autumn.
Lehman Brothers expects additional pension costs of around 40 million stg this quarter. Other analysts believe most exceptionals will hit future quarters.

Most brokers have cut earnings estimates for BT since its American merger partner, MCI Communications Corp, announced an unexpectedly hefty profit warning about two weeks ago. Last year, BT reported pre-tax profits of 3.203 billion pounds. Analysts now expect this year's profits to come in around three billion pounds.
And with no news on how a thorough review by top BT and MCI executives of MCI's businesses is progressing, few brokers are recommending buying BT's shares despite their sharp recent falls.
"We no longer feel that the information flow is sufficient to have us recommend the stock to clients," noted another analyst.

"MCI makes sense -- but at what dilution? I'm not sure BT shareholders can stomach a reduction in earnings for two years in a row when there is no real underlying problem with the UK business," he added.
BT's shares were trading five pence weaker at 414p at 1445 GMT on Friday, well below their year-high of 504p.
